When these characteristics are lacking, or when grave human faults exist with no effort to change, forming a community is impossible.

135 We should also know how to live in mature, responsible freedom with a delicate, but not scrupulous, moral conscience.

Article 2: Life of Prayer

136 The community is founded, above all, on an intense spiritual life:151 daily Mass, adoration of the Blessed Sacrament, Liturgy of the Hours, weekly penitential liturgy,152 weekly chapter, daily Rosary, the Angelus, the Way of the Cross, the wearing of the Scapular, etc.

137 Participation in the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass is the most important act of our day. It is the main act of worship, the sacrifice of praise that gives infinite glory to God. It is in the Mass that Christ, the High and Eternal Priest, perpetuates His redeeming sacrifice on altars all over the world, in such a way that the effects of His Passion reach all men of all times. The Holy Mass is the liturgical act par excellence, and “the liturgy is the summit toward which the activity of the Church is directed; at the same time, it is the font from which all her power flows.”153 From it “grace is poured forth upon us; and the sanctification of men in Christ and the glorification of God, to which all other activities of the Church are directed as toward their end, is achieved in the most efficacious way possible.”154 Therefore, con-celebration of the Holy Mass should be of the utmost importance to the members of the community.

138 “The Canticle of Praise that eternally resounds in the heavens, what Jesus Christ, High Priest, introduced into this world of exile, has been faithfully and constantly continued by the Church.”155 This Canticle of Praise is the Liturgy of the Hours, in which Christ “continues His priestly work through the agency of His Church, which is ceaselessly engaged in praising the Lord and interceding for the salvation of the whole world.”156 The Liturgy of the Hours, “source of piety and nourishment for personal prayer,”157 must be celebrated with the conviction that “all who render this service… by offering these praises to God… are standing before God’s throne in the name of the Church, their Mother.”158 In this prayer, the “necessary complement for the perfect act of divine worship which is the Eucharistic Sacrifice,”159 it is necessary “that… we recognize our own voice in Christ and his own voice in us.”160 If possible, we should try to pray the Lauds (Morning Prayer) and Vespers (Evening Prayer) in common.

139 We should try to have exposition and adoration of the Blessed Sacrament for an hour each day, if possible, as well as Perpetual Adoration in each Province (through turns in each house). “Eucharistic Adoration is the holiest of actions. It is so because it shares the life of Mary on earth, when she adored Him in her womb, in the manger, on the Cross or in the Divine Eucharist, and because it is the perfect exercise of all the virtues: faith, hope and love. Faith is complete and perfect when we adore Jesus Christ hidden, veiled, and as it were, annihilated in the Sacred Host. It is the exercise of hope because Jesus Christ created the beautiful heaven of the Eucharist so that we could wait patiently for the Heaven of Glory and so that he could lead us to it. And it is the exercise of love, since love is the whole law, and we fulfill the whole law when, according to the first commandment, we adore our Lord and God with our whole mind, heart, soul and being. In adoration one can practice perfect charity toward one’s neighbor by praying for him and acting as mediator and victim for his salvation, obtaining for him the Savior’s graces and mercies. Eucharistic Adoration is the most just act: we adore Jesus Christ for all who do not adore Him, for all who forget Him, abandon Him, scorn Him, and offend Him.”161

140 Praying the Holy Rosary, preferably daily, we meditate on the work of the Redemption consummated by Jesus and to which His Mother is intimately linked. “The Holy Rosary is a sacrifice of praise to God for the great gift of our redemption and a holy re-minder of the sufferings, death, and glory of Jesus Christ.”162 “It is an equally universal experience that those who have… great marks of predestination about them love and relish the Hail Mary, and delight in saying it. We always see that the more a man is for God, the more he likes that prayer.… I do not know how it is, nor why, but nevertheless I know well that it is true; nor do I have any better secret of knowing whether a person is for God, then to examine if he likes to say the Hail Mary and the Rosary.”163 The Rosary is a “compendium of the Gospel,”164 an “evangelical prayer centered on the mystery of the redeeming Incarnation,” and in it “the litany repetition of the ‘Hail Mary…’ becomes also a praise to Christ.”165

141 Another practice of piety and veneration of the Blessed Virgin that should characterize us is the Angelus, wherein, “As we commemorate the Incarnation of the Son of God, we ask to be taken by His Passion and cross to the Glory of the resurrection”; in it, we find essential elements such as “the contemplation on the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word, of the greeting to the Virgin, and of recourse to her merciful intercession.”166 The prayer of the Angelus should help us “to renew the consciousness of the Mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God.”167

Article 3: Intellectual Life

142 Intellectual work is another means of encounter in the community; this can take place in the conscientious and intelligent preparation of the Sunday homily, in studying the cases of moral theology that may arise, in studying the ascetics and mystics, and in pastoral planning. We must know how to attain a spirit of recollection and silence, as well as the appropriate use of bibliographies: “Study was for the saints prayer and contemplation.”168 Why did some people, who apparently studied so much, make mistakes? Saint Augustine says, “This way, (the Word) by which they might descend to Him from themselves, they knew not; nor that through Him they might ascend unto Him. This way they knew not, and they think themselves exalted with the stars and shining, and lo! They fell upon the earth, and ‘their senseless minds were darkened’ (Rom 1:21)… the Artificer of the creature, they seek not with devotion, and hence they find Him not… For even when we have a knowledge of these worldly matters, it is folly to make a profession of them; but confession to You is piety.”169

143 We must encourage all ways of access to universal culture, provided they are not disordered; this especially includes access to the knowledge of those considered as the greatest teachers in literature, fine arts, classical and choral music, architecture, the modern visual arts, etc… In the same way, for those members who have the necessary willingness, we encourage knowledge of the different branches of human science: physics, mathematics, astronomy, natural science, medicine, law, social, political, historical, philosophical, philological sciences, and others.

Article 4: Life of Discipline

144 Members of the Institute should live in their own religious house, living life in common, under the authority of the Superior.170

145 As everyone knows, community life demands discipline so that each member can contribute to the good of all. From every point of view, common schedules are necessary for all common activities. The equitable distribution of the “offices” or works of the house is also necessary. Everyone must develop the ministry given to him responsibly and conscientiously.

a. Dialogue with the Superior

146 All religious must turn to their superior frequently and with total confidence. They do this in order to let their superior know about their health, studies, apostolic work, and the difficulties they find in religious life and in the practice of fraternal charity, as well as anything that would contribute to the good of the individuals or the community. The superiors must consider this dialogue as one of their obligations and must always be available to receive and listen to their subjects.

b. Recreation

147 The time dedicated to recreation, or eutrapelia, summer camps, vacations, sports, trips, etc., is worthy of special mention. Especially in small communities, no one should be excused from participation in recreation. Generally, if one does not want to participate cordially in recreation, and if after being corrected there is no change, charitably let him know that he does not have the spirit of our Institute, and dismiss him.

c. Leave of Absence

148 The Institute’s members live in their own religious house and may not be absent without permission of the Superior or whoever acts in his place. According to Canon Law,171 we hereby establish that in the case of a short absence, the local superior can grant permission. In the case of a prolonged absence (diuturnal), the Provincial Superior can give permission; requesting said permission from the superior general is not necessary. We establish that a prolonged absence is one that lasts more than a month. To grant permission for a prolonged absence, the superior needs more than just cause; he also needs the advice and consent of his council. As a general rule, the absence may not be prolonged beyond a year, except in these three anticipated cases:172 illness, studies, or apostolate to be exercised in the name of the Institute.

149 When a religious needs to live permanently outside of the community to carry out certain demands of apostolic life entrusted to the Institute, he must have express permission from the Provincial Superior. The Provincial Superior will approve or deny the request after considering the importance of the mission to be performed and the individual’s spiritual good. In every case, a schedule of visits to the closest community must be established, so as to more easily maintain the fraternal bond. This norm must be understood with regard to an apostolate exercised in the name of the Institute, and not to a personal apostolate freely chosen by the religious.

150 When a religious feels sick, he must communicate this to his superior and submit to the superior’s command with complete detachment and Ignatian indifference.

151 Except for the aforementioned three cases of illness, apostolate, or studies, for an absence longer than a year, we should consider seeking an indult of exclaustration.173 Illegitimate absence for more than a semester is grounds for cause to be dismissed from the Institute.174

d. Use of Media

152 We must be very discerning in the use of media. In general it disturbs an authentic life of prayer and study. Whatever we read, see, and hear should always be done with a critical spirit. The inappropriate use of TV, Internet, etc., is destructive to our communities because it fills the soul with things that are not God. Members are to rigorously avoid “whatever is harmful to their own vocation and dangerous to the chastity of a consecrated person.”175

e. Enclosure

153 An enclosure must be maintained in every house, so that one part of the house is for the exclusive use of the religious. This space should be appropriately adapted in each house according to its own rule. This also applies to the monasteries.176

f. Habit

154 The religious of our Institute must wear the holy habit, which is a sign of their consecration and a witness to their poverty.177 The value of the habit is given “not only because it contributes to the propriety of the priest in his external behavior or in the exercise of his ministry, but above all because it gives evidence within the ecclesiastical community of the public witness that each priest is to give of his own identity and special belonging to God.”178 Now more than ever, signs must be utilized, “especially in today’s world, so sensitive to the language of images… where the sense of the sacred has been so terribly weakened; people need these elements that cry out to God, that cannot be disregarded without an impoverishment of our priestly service.”179 This sign “expresses for the religious his consecration and makes evident the eschatological end of religious life.”180 Therefore, let us love the habit, which should be like our very skin. Saint Francis of Assisi said that the simple presence of a religious dressed in the holy habit was a way of preaching.181

Article 5: Pastoral Life

155 Pastoral life is oriented “to communicate the charity of Christ.”182 It must have a special emphasis, because when carried out in an orderly manner, it eminently fosters community life.

156 Pastoral work is a cross for us, not an escape. This is why we must never succumb to unproductive activism, as “the activity for the Lord must not let us forget Who is the Lord of the activity.”183

157 In the weekly chapters, after the first point on Spirituality and the second on the faults, there must be a third point to organize, among other things, the pastoral work. Nobody should assume any commitment (Masses, preaching, etc.) without the explicit permission of the superior or his delegate, as he is the one who must coordinate these apostolic works.

158 We should know how to transition from a passive ministry to an active ministry, from a bureaucratic ministry to a ministry that will effectively reach everyone. Except for the enclosure, have the doors open so that the lay faithful may come to consult us. According to the area, the church doors especially should be kept open. However, if there is danger, prudently seek out some type of security measure. Unless there are truly grave and unsolvable circumstances, the people of God ought to have easy access to Jesus present in the Tabernacle.

159 We should always be with the poor, above all giving them food. We should not be afraid of not having enough for ourselves. God is never outdone in generosity. The superior should take care of every aspect of tending to the poor. In some cases, this may mean not only assisting the urgent works of mercy, but also promoting long-term works of justice.

160 We have to take on the modern Areopagi that are open to the Church’s activity without abandoning the traditional methods of apostolate. Healthy creativity is an essential element of the living Church tradition. We must not be afraid; Christ Himself invites us to “put out into the deep.”184 This principle always re-mains true, “for the same God is now that was then.”185

PART 6 APOSTOLATE

Article 1: Sending

161 The risen Christ, King of the Universe, sends His apostles to all nations to continue His own redeeming mission which “is to enable people to share in the communion that exists between the Father and the Son.”186 Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you (Mt 28:19-20).

162 This sending has two characteristics:

- A universal dimension: all men are called to be a part of the Kingdom of God, since God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4).

- The certainty of divine help: I am with you always, to the close of the age (Mt 28:20); they went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them… (Mk 16:20).

Article 2: Proclamation of the Kingdom

163 In virtue of this sending, the Church’s mission is the proclamation of the Kingdom of God. “The kingdom of God is not a concept, a doctrine, or a program subject to free interpretation, but it is before all else a person with the face and name of Jesus of Nazareth, the image of the invisible God.”187 The Church carries out this mission to liberate men from sin and death: When you were dead [in] transgressions… he brought you to life along with him, having forgiven us all our transgressions (Col 2:13). The principal promoter is the Holy Spirit, who acts in the Apostles and in the whole Church.188

164 That is why fidelity to the Holy Spirit permits us to overcome all the difficulties that the Church finds in her mission: prohibition against evangelization, obstacles from local cultures, lack of fervor, divisions among Christians, de-Christianization in countries of long-standing Christian tradition, a decrease in missionary vocations, a poor witness of the faithful, indifferent mentalities, and others.189 It is the Holy Spirit who guides us to the complete truth.190

Article 3: Witnessing

165 The Church’s mission is carried out by every Christian, and in a particular way, by those who have consecrated themselves to God in apostolate. Their purpose is identical to the Church’s purpose: to bring all men to conversion to God, to “a complete and sincere adherence to Christ and His Gospel through faith,”191 which must result in the worthy reception of the Sacraments.

166 In this apostolic work where “we are missionaries above all because of what we are… even before we become missionaries in word or deed,”192 our testimony of life – the “first and irreplaceable form of mission”193 – occupies the first place so that the charity of Christ may shine among the faithful.194

167 Preaching is an essential element of this work of apostolate, i.e. “a clear proclamation that Jesus Christ offers salvation to all men,”195 because, how can they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach? …Thus faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ (Rom 10:14- 17).

168 In a particular way, there is an urgent necessity for apostolic endeavors in the so-called “modern Areopagi.” In these new environments, we first find the world of communication, upon which the work of evangelizing modern culture greatly depends. This world of communication is “unifying humanity and turning it into what is known as a ‘global village’… The means of social communication have become so important as to be for many the chief means of information and education... In particular, the younger generation is growing up in a world conditioned by the mass media.”196 Particularly “we must also mention the immense Areopagus of culture, scientific research, and international relations which promote dialogue and open up new possibilities,”197 such as the commitment to peace, to development, to human rights, and the longing for interior life and prayer. “While on the one hand people seem to be pursuing material prosperity and to be sinking ever deeper into consumerism and materialism, on the other hand we are witnessing a desperate search for meaning, the need for an inner life, and a desire to learn new forms and methods of meditation and prayer… This phenomenon – the so-called ‘religious revival’ – is not without ambiguity, but it also represents an opportunity. The Church has an immense spiritual patrimony to offer humankind, a heritage in Christ, who called himself the way, and the truth, and the life (Jn 14:6).”198

Article 4: Apostolic Commitments

169 The Institute of the Incarnate Word will take on the works of apostolate most conducive to the inculturization of the Gospel. For this reason, there are various Directories that complement the Constitutions. These Directories deal with apostolic action in the most urgent and important fields.

170 We list the preferred fields of apostolate here:

171 a) Spiritual dimension. The Institute will accomplish evangelization of the culture by sanctifying people individually. This will be done preferably by using the Spiritual Exercises according to the method and spirit of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and by spiritual direction.

172 b) Intellectual dimension. The Institute gives priority to: priestly formation in seminaries; education on all levels; the formation of lay leaders by means of courses in Catholic culture; the media.

173 c) Pastoral dimension. Preference will be given to helping parishes through preaching (tridua, novenas, feasts of patron saints), and the administration of the Sacrament of Reconciliation. Another priority is the outreach mission in parishes and in rural areas according to the method and spirit of Saint Alphonsus Liguori, in all its forms: intensive mission; ongoing mission; missions preached to the youth and children, the sick, factory workers; open missions, etc. In response to Bishops’ requests, the Institute can accept the direction of parishes, preferably in missionary areas or those in greater need. We will be attentive to respect, rescue, and elevate the religious and ethnic traditions proper to each place, so that the Gospel will be better received and become more deeply rooted in peoples’ hearts.

174 d) Charitable works. We must give privileged attention to the poor, sick, and all those in need: the love of Christ impels us (2 Cor 5:14), practicing concrete charity, witnessing first to the members of our Institute that “charity, and only charity, will save the world. Blessed are those who have the grace of being victims of charity!”199 In order to evangelize the culture, charity is essential, for it is both the end of the one who works and the end of the work itself; otherwise, the “civilization of love”200 will not be reached.

Article 5: Second and Third Orders

175 In our apostolic work, special preference will be given to the spiritual care of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará according to their needs. “Special care” will be given to the institutions, associations, movements and members of the lay Third Order, so that they might be formed in the spirit of our Religious Family.201

176 Any members of our Institute dedicated to spiritual apostolate should be convinced that the sanctification of the laity is of immense value to the Church’s life. The works and examples of the great masters of Catholic pastoral ministry will be the foundation of their apostolate.

177 Unless they ask to be excluded, we regard all those who ever belonged to our Institute as members of the Brotherhood or Confraternity of the Incarnate Word, including those who try to harm us. Even if they do ask to be excluded, we are obligated to pray for them and to do good to them. The fact that they leave our Institute does not mean that they are no longer our beloved brothers.

Article 6: Educational Apostolate

178 Any religious dedicated to education will try to immerse themselves in an absolute and total love for the truth. They will work such that the Gospel principles may effectively influence the lives of men. In a world that believes that error possesses the same rights as truth, they will combat errors with all their strength. They will give a privileged place to the Magisterium of the Church, to the doctrine of the Church Fathers and to the teachings of Saint Thomas Aquinas, a place that the Popes, the Second Vatican Council, and the Code of Canon Law give to them in theological disciplines. In philosophy they will teach the contribution of the ancient Greeks received into the Catholic tradition that has rightly been called the “philosophical heritage that is perennially valid.”202

179 Those who are dedicated to theological, philosophical, scientific, and cultural research, or to research in other fields, should have a very clear understanding that, though seemingly distant, this intellectual work is not only for the greater glory of God, but also for the greater good of souls. They must understand that their work fully belongs to the charism of our Institute. Saint Thomas says, “We must consider that in any art the one who arranges the art and is called the architect is absolutely better than any manual laborer who carries out what is designed for him by another. So also in constructing buildings, the one who designs the building, although he does no work with his hands, is contracted for greater pay than the manual workers who hew the wood and cut the stones. But in a spiritual building there are manual workers, as it were, who particularly pursue the guidance of souls, e.g. by administering the sacraments or by doing certain other things. But the bishops are like the principal artisans who command and arrange how the mentioned workers ought to conduct their duties, which is why they are called “episcopi,” i.e. superintendents. And likewise teachers of theology are like principal craftsmen who inquire and teach how others ought to procure the salvation of souls. Therefore, it is absolutely better to teach theology and more meritorious if it is done with good intention, than to devote particular care to the salvation of this one and that… Reason itself also demonstrates that it is better to teach salvationrelated matters to those who can benefit from it both for themselves and others, than to [teach] simple people who can only benefit from it themselves.”203

180 Keeping in mind the particular benefits of intellectual apostolate, we will give special attention to spreading the Gospel through articles in investigative journals, periodicals, essays, books, and other kinds of publications. What is written remains and is more widely disseminated.

Article 7: Pastoral Work in Parishes

181 The religious who take care of parishes should give priority, with enthusiastic pastoral action, to the following:

- The Sunday liturgy, with a conscientiously-prepared homily. The center of the parish pastoral work should always be the Sunday Mass, [and our members should] work especially to promote the solemnity of the celebration so that the faithful will participate knowingly, devoutly and actively.204 This should be complemented by bringing communion to the sick.

- Availability to hear confessions at any time. We should be willing to offer authentic spiritual direction. We should know how to guide those who are predisposed to the practice of the Spiritual Exercises. We should assume the responsibility of teaching catechism to children and adults.

- We should create appropriate lay associations, so that all faithful lay Christians can work in an apostolate, with both diversity and unity, according to their own charisms and willingness. Children and youth should be looked after according to the spirit of Saint Philip Neri and Saint John Bosco. The “Oratory” is still relevant.

- The central moments for the parochial pastoral work will be: Holy Week, Feasts of Patron Saints, First Communions, Confirmations, outreach mission, and courses on Catholic culture.

Article 8: Preachers

182 Religious who are dedicated to the pastoral care of parishes located in the neediest of places, and to the preaching in outreach missions, will become a continuation of the redemptive work of Christ Himself through their actions. To better fulfill their mission, they must be convinced that the best way to develop an efficient apostolate is to live in intimate union with the Incarnate Word and to love souls to the point of sacrificing themselves with heroism and without reserve. We must have a special appreciation for the teaching of the great masters of sacred preaching, particularly in regard to how the preaching should be done.205 “All those who announce the Word, are the voice of the Word.”206

Article 9: Selection of Ministries

183 The Superior General can send any member of the Institute to anywhere there is a need. In the selection of ministries, we must take into account the wise provisions given by Saint Ignatius of Loyola.207

184 Workers are needed everywhere. Therefore, a selection process in sending missionaries becomes necessary. The place, objective, number of people sent and how to send them, those to be sent, the length of the assignment, and other circumstances will be taken into account. We must weigh the advantages and inconveniences, and seek only the greater glory of God and the common good; we must pray and ask others to pray, ask for advice from prudent persons and decide in God’s presence according to a right conscience.

185 The one who is sent should have no preference about going to one place or another, since God is in all places. He will put his assignment totally and freely in the hands of his superior who takes the place of Christ our Lord. The superior will have to guide him in the way of greater service and praise of God. The religious must absolutely avoid influencing the superior’s will regarding the provision of any assignment. In the Church there are no assignments that are places of punishment; therefore, neither are there any in our Institute. If anyone thinks the contrary, he does not know the Church or the Institute.

186 In addition, in order to always seek the greater glory of God and the universal good, the following rules must be considered when sending missionaries. We prefer to send missionaries:

a) Wherever there is a greater need for missionaries, either because of the lack of missionaries or because the faithful are in urgent need of them.

b) Where there will be more fruit for the Glory of God, by having more facilities, more willingness of the faithful to take advantage of the mission (which may be judged by an insistent re-quest for missionaries), and where there are more compatible conditions and qualities in which to develop and preserve the anticipated spiritual fruits.

c) Wherever we owe a debt of gratitude, for example, wherever more vocations have come from, or where we have more benefactors; wherever, in fact, God has planted us, there we must flourish.

d) Since the more universal goodness is, the more divine it is, we must prefer those who, because of their authority, can spread goodness to many others; including government leaders, professionals, teachers, intellectuals, entrepreneurs, managers, artists, and many others. For example, evangelizing the Secretary of the Treasury who, once converted, will justly eradicate all slums, is preferable to trying to solve each individual problem. However, both aspects must be considered.

e) Wherever there is more evil sown against our Institute, including bad opinion or bad will; with their lives and doctrine, missionaries would change those misinformed prejudices.

f) Wherever there is something that concerns our Institute in a particular way, or wherever there is no one else to take care of that ministry, always giving preference to those ministries that would benefit the most and endure the longest.

g) Wherever there are responsibilities of great importance, and to these missions we should choose to send the people we trust the most. Likewise, strong and healthy people should be appointed to places where there is need of more pastoral work. Solid people who have been proven in virtue may be sent where there are more spiritual dangers.

187 Those who are outstanding in discretion and prudence should be appointed to govern, whereas those who have talent for preaching and hearing confessions should be appointed to work with the people.

188 Sending one member by himself to a mission is not advisable. At least two members should be sent, so that they can help each other in their spiritual and material matters. One of them should have more experience than the other, so as to be imitated and consulted for advice. Sending a cheerful and fervent member with another more prudent and tranquil member is most appropriate, so that the differences can balance and help each other. In a mission of greater importance, more missionaries must be sent.

189 h) When sending or transferring someone, we must keep in mind: the importance of the spiritual work, the obligation to go there, the ability of the Institute to provide what is needed in those places, as well as the fruits we expect to obtain, where the Institute is now working and where the missionary will be sent.

190 i) Motions or considerations against going to a particular mission can be presented to the Superior by any member of the Institute. However, the member must always submit himself to the Superior’s will.

191 j) The Superior must give clear instructions regarding the office and place chosen for the member. Likewise, the member must appropriately submit information about anything needed, so that the Superior can provide the necessities of the mission to them. This should be done even when the member is well-instructed and experienced. Reporting on these matters in detail is a serious obligation, and should be done at least once a year by means of the “annual letter.”

Article 10: Rest

192 All members of the Institute will interrupt their apostolic work with periods of retreat and spiritual refreshment. No one can provide sanctification to other souls if he is not working to acquire the perfection he wants to transmit.

Article 11: Keystones

193 All members of the Institute participate – each one in his own capacity – in the apostolic mission of the congregation, even when they perform works that do not strictly deal with souls. Likewise, sick and elderly religious participate fully by their sufferings in the apostolate exercised by the other members, because they are completing what is lacking in the passion of the Lord.208

194 The sick and the elderly, together with the members of the contemplative branch, the coadjutor brothers, and those who are dedicated to works of mercy, are the cornerstones of the apostolic endeavor of our Institute.

PART 7 FORMATION OF MEMBERS

CHAPTER 1 DIMENSIONS OF THE FORMATION

195 We want to form the members of our Institute in human and Christian maturity so that they reach the extent of the full stature of Christ (Eph 4:13).

With their works, members should demonstrate that they have God in their hearts because every tree is known by its own fruit (Lk 6:44), and faith, if it has no works, is dead (Jas 2:17).

We can organize this work into four sections: Human formation; Spiritual formation; Intellectual formation; Apostolic and pastoral formation. Nothing is better on this topic than the teachings of Blessed John Paul II,209 which we embrace as our own.

Article 1: Human Formation

196 Human formation is the basis of religious and priestly formation. Misunderstanding the relationship between nature and grace is the root of many evils. Grace does not destroy nature, but rather heals it, raises it, perfects it, dignifies it, and ennobles it. Nature is not only the foundation of grace, as though it were a mere external condition, but it belongs to the very essence of Christian identity and remains perfected. At the same time, grace transcends nature. Nature is subordinate to grace, as the obediential potency to its perfective act. Thus the natural has relative autonomy subordinate to the supernatural.

197 Because of the greater demands of his vocation, the priest should reflect – as should every Christian – the Incarnation of the Word, in whom human perfection and divine perfection shine, in intimate union but without blending together. Moreover, the priest, taken from among men and made their representative before God (Heb 5:1), must serve as a bridge, and not as an obstacle to others; he should make his ministry acceptable and believable from a human standpoint.

198 He “should be able to know the depths of the human heart, to perceive difficulties and problems, to make meetings and dialogue easy, to create trust and cooperation, to express serene and objective judgments.” Therefore, there is a need “for them to be balanced people, strong and free.”210

- Balanced: we must be priests who remain focused on the whole and not on just a single part, who don’t become overlyexcited with what they consider the whole; they must not let themselves be overcome by a depressive attitude that sees more evil than good, and must instead make room in their soul for all things, without despising or minimizing anything, but with hierarchy and order.

- Strong: we must be priests who do not allow ourselves to be carried away by every wind of doctrine and novelty, priests who move ourselves and judge by principles, who are neither softhearted and sentimental, nor hard and aloof.

- Free: we must be priests who do everything out of love, who do good even when no one is obliges them, or because the Superior is watching, nor on account of commendations or rewards. We must not be obsequious with the superiors, or try to obtain advantages. As priests, we should know how to implement fraternal correction, without caring about what others think of us, and understand with Saint Teresa of Jesus “the nothingness of the world and how it would soon come to an end.”211

199 “They need to be educated to love the truth, to be loyal, to respect everyone, to have a sense of justice, to be true to their word, to be genuinely compassionate, to be men of integrity, and especially, to be balanced in judgment and behavior.”212 Education for the love of truth must be carried out via extensive intellectual formation, which is ordered to the truth and is unsatisfied with mere theological opinions. It must be a philosophical formation, as Saint Justin understood it. This formation will include theorizing, intellectual leisure, and sincere debate, which is a shared search for truth. Classes need to be moments in which true teaching and learning take place. “A simple and demanding program for this human formation can be found in the words of the apostle Paul to the Philippians: Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is gracious, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things (Phil 4:8).”213

200 Along with intellectual formation, the will must be appropriately formed through constant practice of the virtues and control of passions, so that we are seeking and choosing only the greater good, always and everywhere. We want to form men who are authentically free and masters of themselves, who by that self-mastery are capable of giving themselves totally. We regard the practice of sports, camping, community vacations, etc., to be of great importance in this formation of the will.

Article 2: Spiritual Formation

201 The supernatural end of man corresponds to the natural end, but at the same time, transcends it: man’s desires are completely brought to rest in the beatific vision.214 During the time of formation, we must keep in mind this correspondence and transcendence. Pius XI teaches, “The Christian education encompasses the entire human life… to elevate, regulate, and perfect it according to the example and doctrine of Christ.”215

202 Spiritual life must be understood “as a relationship and communion with God.”216 “Spiritual training …should be imparted in such a way that students might learn to live in an intimate and unceasing union with the Father through His Son Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit.”217 Therefore, spiritual life is a form of friendship: I no longer call you slaves, because a slave does not know what his master is doing. I have called you friends, because I have told you everything I have heard from my Father (Jn 15:15). This friendship has the characteristics of a true search:218 the priest must have an unquenchable thirst for God. He must never oppose “the search for the truth and the certainty of already knowing the fountain of this truth.”219 This search is possible because in some way we have already found the truth; however, we must make our relationship even more intimate. There is a threefold path to this encounter:220 meditation on the Word of God; participation in the Sacred Mysteries; fraternal charity, especially with those most in need.

203 - Faithful meditation on the Word of God is how we know the divine mysteries and make its values our own. This is particularly related to prophetic ministry.221 We take to heart the teaching of the Second Vatican Council: “All clerics, particularly priests of Christ and others who, as deacons or catechists, are officially engaged in the ministry of the Word, should immerse themselves in the Scriptures by constant sacred reading and diligent study. For it must not happen that anyone becomes an empty preacher of the Word of God to others, not being a hearer of the Word in his own heart.”222 The response to lectio divina is prayer, “which is without any doubt of primary value and a demand of spiritual formation…” because “the priest is the man of God, the one who belongs to God and makes people think about God.” Moreover, “one aspect of the priest’s mission, and certainly by no means a secondary aspect, is to become a ‘teacher of prayer’”; therefore, “the priest needs to be formed to have a deep intimacy with God.”223 The fruits of this intimacy with God and of the work of the Holy Spirit in the soul of the priest are discernment, relishing the presence of God, accepting His will, and rightly judging matters.224

204 - Active participation in the Sacred Mysteries, especially the Eucharist, which “is the source and summit of Christian prayer,”225 must also be a part of the formation. An authentic liturgical education is necessary for this participation, which increasingly brings one to a “full, conscious and active”226 participation in it. Above all, priests are the ministers of the Sacrifice of the Mass227 because of their condition as ministers of the sacred things: his “role is utterly irreplaceable, because without the priest there can be no Eucharistic offering.”228 Therefore, seminarians must participate daily in the Eucharistic celebration. They must regard it as the most essential moment of the day, when they identify themselves with the sacrificed Christ himself.

205 Furthermore, they must discover the beauty and joy of the Sacrament of Penance, amid a world that has lost a sense of sin and divine mercy.229 Additionally, and in order to practice “the ‘radical self-giving’ proper to the priest following the example of Christ the good shepherd… it is necessary to inculcate the meaning of the cross, which is at the heart of the paschal mystery.”230

206 - We need formation in fraternal charity, especially toward those most in need. We have to teach those in formation to look for Christ in all men. “The priest is a man of charity and is called to educate others according to Christ’s example and the new commandment of brotherly love (cf. Jn 15:12). But this re-quires that he allow himself to be constantly trained by the Spirit in the charity of Christ. In this sense preparation for the priesthood must necessarily involve a proper formation in charity, and particularly in the preferential love for the ‘poor’ in whom our faith discovers Jesus (Mt 25:40), and a merciful love for sinners.”231 This charity in the priest springs forth from prayer and from contemplating the mystery of divine mercy.

207 According to this view of charity, “which consists of the loving gift of oneself, the following should be found in the program of spiritual formation of the future priest: education in obedience, celibacy and poverty.”232 “Students should clearly understand that it is not intended for them to dominate people or to receive honors from them but to give themselves over totally to the service of God and to pastoral ministry. With particular concern they should be so formed in priestly obedience, in a simple way of life and in the spirit of self-denial, that they are accustomed to willingly giving up even those things which are permitted but are not expedient, and to conform themselves to Christ crucified.”233

208 Furthermore, living the proper charism of the Institute must be instilled in them.234

209 Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Blessed Virgin, must be the center of our entire spiritual life. No one comes to the Father but by me (Jn 14:6). In the temple, the cloister, the cell, the dining room, and at recreation, we must always be crying out for Christ. The song and laughter of the members of our Religious Family must be like cries for Jesus Christ. This is our duty. The sweeter the melody we sing in the choir, the better will the profound and interior sigh of our souls crying out for Jesus Christ be made manifest. The memory and recollection of Him must never be separated from our hearts. It must come when we sleep and when we dream. Our heart is always falling in love, and our memory must never be occupied by anything but Him.235

210 Christ became flesh in order that we might have life and have it more abundantly (Jn 10:10). To have this life in Jesus Christ,236 it is absolutely essential to be united with His Person, have His Spirit, assimilate His doctrine, frequent His sacraments, imitate His example, profoundly love His Mother, and be in perfect communion with the Church hierarchy by a double bond: by faith and charity themselves, and by the governance of one, Peter, over all.

211 Our motto is “with Peter and under Peter.”237

212 We want to form virtuous men (that is, “virtuous” in the sense of vir and vis: to have the strength of the man) according to the doctrine of the great teachers of spiritual life, especially Saint Augustine, Saint Thomas Aquinas, Saint John of the Cross, Saint Teresa of Jesus, Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Saint Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort, Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus, and according to the examples of all the saints of all times that the Church proposes as models of virtue for us to imitate.

213 In this way, following the Holy Father in belief and following the saints in practice, we will never err, since, just as the Holy Father cannot err in his teachings about faith and morals, nor did the saints err in their practice of the virtues.

214 We want to form priestly souls of priests who are not “tributaries,”238 priests who will fully live the Christian and priestly kingship and lordship. Since they have Jesus Christ, may they feel this phrase resounding in their ears: “I am your Father because I am God, I am your firstborn brother because I am man. I am your payment and ransom. Why do you fear debts, if you with penance and confession beg to be absolved of them? I am your reconciliation. Why do you fear wrath? I am the bond of friendship. Why fear the anger of God? I am your defender. Why fear adversaries? I am your friend. Why are you afraid of lacking what I have, if you do not separate from me? My Body and my Blood are yours. Why do you fear hunger? My heart is yours. Why do you fear forgetfulness? My divinity is yours. Why do you fear miseries? And for further assistance, my angels are yours to defend you; my saints are yours to pray for you; my blessed Mother is yours to be your attentive and pious Mother; the earth is yours for you to serve Me on it, the heavens are yours because you will come to them; the devils and hell are yours, because you will humiliate them as slaves in prison; life is yours because with it, you win what lasts forever; good pleasures are yours because you offer them to Me; hardships are yours because for My love and your [own] profit, you suffer them; temptations are yours because they are the merits and cause of your eternal crown; death is yours because it will be your nearest transition to life. And all this you possess in Me and for Me, because I have gained this not for Me alone, neither do I want to enjoy this alone; because when I entered into fellowship with you in the flesh, I assumed it to make you partakers in what I would work on, fast, eat, sweat and weep, [participants] in My pains and in My deaths, if it was not given to you to do. You who have so much wealth are not poor, if you who lead a bad life, do not want to lose it knowingly.”239

215 We religious must be convinced, as St. John of the Cross was, that “mine are the heavens and mine is the earth. Mine are the nations, the just are mine, and mine the sinners. The angels are mine, and the Mother of God, and all things are mine, and God himself is mine and for me, because Christ is mine and all for me.”240 Our religious must understand and live that vibrant expression of Saint Paul: Everything belongs to you, Paul or Apollos or Cephas, or the world or life or death, or the present or the future: all belong to you, and you to Christ, and Christ to God (1 Cor 3:21-23).

216 One aspect of spiritual formation should be to acquire discipline of life, a goal that means to grasp the “style” of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the attitudes that He has as the Son next to the Father. Discipline in our relationship with Him as disciples means understanding Him as our “path” to the Father. Discipline is the fundamental attitude of the disciple. It is a submission to the rules of life so that the truth may become flesh in the disciple’s life. For us, the truth is Christ, and being docile to discipline means letting Him be our Lord.

217 We want to be docile to the Church’s great discipline, which is expressed in the Code of Canon Law and in all ecclesiastical rules and laws, and to be docile to the particular discipline of our Institute, remembering the teaching, “Apprehendite disciplinam.” Thus it is written: Embrace discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry (Ps 2:12),241 as well by the Apostle: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Eph 6:4). In this way, the members of the Institute will become useful to the master of the house (2 Tim 2:21). “To educate them in discipline is nothing but to induce them to good.”242 In this way, the brothers “show their own style of life.”243

218 The discipline of the Institute is contained: in a general way in its good customs and traditions, as well as in the collection of regulations of its proper law that orders the life of members and communities. These solidify the spirit of the Institute in everyday life, and in a particular way, it is the collection of practical norms contained in the Directories and Regulations.

Article 3: Intellectual Formation

219 The intellectual formation of future priests is an urgent issue facing the New Evangelization and the subject of modern challenges. This formation “is a fundamental demand of human intelligence by which one “participates in the light of God’s mind” and seeks to acquire a wisdom, which in turn opens to and is directed toward knowing and adhering to God.”244 This formation includes two phases, one ordered to the other: the study of philosophy, and the study of the Sacred Science.

220 “A crucial stage of intellectual formation is the study of philosophy, which leads to a deeper understanding and interpretation of the person, and of the person’s freedom and relationships with the world and with God.”245 This study is urgent, not only in view of later theological studies, but also in light of a particular cultural situation that exalts subjectivism as the criteria and measure of the truth.246 A “certainty of the truth” is necessary, and this is given only by a sound philosophy, founded in the objective re-ality of things, since “intelligence… is able to arrive at what is.”247 Without it, there is no basis for a total personal abandonment to Jesus and the Church since, “If you are not sure about the truth, how can we risk our own life and be strong enough to seriously question the life of others?”248 That is why the study of philosophy leads the future priest to lovingly embrace the truth, which in turn leads him to recognize that this truth is not created and measured by man, but granted to him as a gift by the Supreme Truth, God. Human reason, even with limitations and difficulties, can reach objective universal truth, even in reference to God and existence in its radical sense. He must learn that faith itself cannot do without reason or the effort to ponder over the contents of faith, as Saint Augustine attested: “I have wished to see with understanding what I have believed by faith, and I have debated and worked hard.”249

221 In intellectual formation, the beginning and end is Jesus Christ, especially Jesus Christ as He is known through Sacred Scripture. He is the light of the Paginae Sacrae: He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Lk 24:45). Understanding the Bible is a grace from Christ: Their thoughts were rendered dull, for to this present day the same veil remains unlifted when they read the old covenant, because through Christ it is taken away (2 Cor 3:14). He is the center of the Sacred Scriptures as He, Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, … interpreted to them what referred to him in all the scriptures (Lk 24:27). Thus, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”250 Therefore, Sacred Scripture is the “soul” of theology.251

222 The reading of Sacred Scripture should be done “in church”252 because: …No prophesy of the scripture is a matter of one’s own interpretation (2 Pt 1:20). The strictest fidelity to the Supreme Magisterium of the Church of all times, the proximate norm of faith, is absolutely necessary.

223 Intellectual formation of the future priest “is based and built above all on the study of sacred doctrine and theology”253 that comes from faith and tries to lead us to faith, as the Magisterium of the Church and Catholic theologians have always taught. Saint Thomas teaches that faith is the “habitus” of theology, that is to say, its permanent operative principle,254 and that all theology is ordained to nourish the faith.255 Indeed, what a great need we have to enter into the mysteries of the faith by means of theological studies, as we are called to be men of faith who should bring our brethren to, and strengthen them in, the faith!

224 Theological reflection “is centered on adherence to Jesus Christ, the wisdom of God. In addition to helping candidates grow in scientific precision, [it] will also help them develop a great and living love for Jesus Christ and for his Church.”256 That love nourishes spiritual life and serves as a model for the generous exercise of ministry. Therefore, theology must be nourished by prayer and by the love of Jesus Christ. Saint Bonaventure points out, “May no one believe that reading without unction is enough, nor speculation without devotion, searching without amazement, observation without joy, activity without piety, science without charity, intelligence without humility, studies without divine grace, investigation without wisdom coming from supernatural inspiration.”257

225 This study must lead to “a complete and unified vision of the truths which God has revealed in Jesus Christ and of the Church’s experience of faith. Hence arises the need both to know all the Christian truths, without arbitrarily selecting among them, and to know them in an orderly fashion.”258

226 In reflecting on faith, theology moves in two directions: first is the study of the Word of God, written in the Sacred Books, celebrated and transmitted in the living Tradition of the Church and authentically interpreted by the Magisterium. This study of Sacred Scripture includes not only the Fathers of the Church who explained the recorded deeds and words of God,259 but also liturgy, Church history, and magisterial declarations. The second direction is that of man, “the interlocutor of God,” who is called to live, believe, and communicate the Christian faith. From this comes the study of dogmatic, moral, pastoral, and spiritual theology, as well as of Canon Law.260

227 We will give preference to the works of Saint Thomas Aquinas, because we have to be formed “under his magisterium,”261 and hold him “especially as a teacher”262 for the following reasons: he “illumined the Church more than all the other doctors. In his books, one profits more in only one year than in the study of all the others during his whole life.”263 He “most venerated the ancient doctors of the Church, [and] in a certain way he seems to have inherited the intellect of all.”264 The “Church has proclaimed that the doctrine of Saint Thomas is her own.”265 God has willed that by the strength and truth of the doctrine of the Angelic Doctor, “All the heresies and error that would follow will be driven away, confounded and condemned.”266 His knowledge is of undeniable and fundamental importance for the right interpretation of Sacred Scripture, so as to transcend the sensory and achieve union with God, and to build the edifice of Sacred Theology upon the solid base provided by a profound knowledge of the philosophy of being – a “perennially valid philosophical heritage”267 – and the advances of philosophical investigation.

Article 4: Pastoral Formation

228 Jesus Christ is also the end here, as Chief Shepherd (1 Pt 5:4), for He is the Supreme Model, and the flock is His: Tend my sheep (Jn 21:16). That is why “the whole formation imparted to candidates to the priesthood aims at preparing them to communicate the charity of Christ, the Good Shepherd.”268 Since our Institute has an apostolic branch, pastoral endeavors are essential to it. We must never forget that there is no authentic Catholic pastoral work without a profound spiritual life, without solid doctrinal formation, and without manly discipline.

229 A thirst for souls must be part of the vocation from the very beginning of religious life that gradually and prudently cements itself in the life of the candidate, the novice, and the professed. This is why pastoral formation should include an initial and progressive experience in ministry.269

230 Here, formation ends in Christ alone, Christ always, Christ in everything, Christ in all, and All Christ, until the religious can truly say, Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Cor 11:1) and, it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (Gal 2:20). In such a way Jesus Christ will defend us before the Father on Judgment Day, “See that he is my member and he is me.”270

231 We aspire to form priests for the Catholic Church according to the Heart of Christ, priests who nourish their spirit with the Word of God, serve their neighbor in solidarity with all in need, promote the laity, and have a great capability for dialogue without suffering any identity crisis. Our priests must desire ongoing formation, abandon themselves to Providence, and love the Catholic liturgy. These individuals are tireless preachers, “rich in spirit,”271 “with tongue, lips, and wisdom, which the enemies of truth cannot resist,”272 who are exceptionally fruitful in their apostolic and vocational efforts; they have missionary and ecumenical impetus, are open to any particle of truth wherever it is found, have preferential love for the poor without exclusivity and without exclusions. They must live in transparent and contagious joy, in unperturbed peace even amid the most arduous battles; they live in absolute and unrestricted ecclesiastical communion as re-lentless evangelists and catechists and as lovers of the cross. In short, we seek to form priests who are men with common sense, with that Christian common sense, which is none other than a familiarity with the Word made flesh.

CHAPTER 2 STAGES OF FORMATION Article 1: Minor Seminary

232 The first stage of formation is the minor seminary. The minor seminary is for all those who demonstrate a desire to devote themselves to God at an early age. “The goal of the minor seminary is to help those adolescents who have manifested the seed of a vocation, to discern more easily and to be able to re-spond to it.”273

At the end of his studies at the minor seminary, the candidate, “having a clear conscience of the divine call… may have reached the human and spiritual maturity that permits him to make the decision to respond to the call with sufficient responsibility and freedom.”274

233 “As experience has long shown, a priestly vocation tends to manifest itself in the preadolescent years or in the earliest years of youth. Even in those who decide to enter the seminary later, it is not uncommon to find that God’s call had been perceived much earlier.”275 In considering Jesus’ predilection for the apostle John, Saint Thomas taught, “This gives us an understanding of how God loves in a special way those who give themselves to his service from an early age.”276

234 In the minor seminary superiors must instill in the candidate who desires to consecrate himself to God a “special religious formation that disposes him to follow Christ the Redeemer – poor, chaste and obedient – with the spirit of generosity and purity of intention,”277 particularly by means of “adequate spiritual direction.”278

We have to ensure, therefore, that the seminarians “mature harmoniously in their physical, moral, and intellectual qualities and in their affections.”279 The work of the superiors does not exclude the “appropriate cooperation of the parents.”280

235 For appropriate formation of seminarians, we must teach them to value and love: the mystery of the Holy Eucharist, which must be the center of their whole life, particularly in the Holy Mass; the Sacrament of Reconciliation; prompt and joyous obedience; the Holy Virgin Mary and the saints who are intercessors and models of life. Holy Scripture, as it has been written, From infancy you have known the sacred scriptures, which are capable of giving you wisdom for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Tim 3:15); “Christ known, searched for, and loved more and more through one’s studies, personal sacrifices, victories over one’s self, in the slow conquest of the virtues of justice, fortitude, temperance and prudence; Christ contemplated with fervent and patient perseverance in order that… there will be imprinted upon them the same face of Christ (cf. 2 Cor 3:18).”281

Article 2: Postulancy

236 The period of postulancy is a time of first contacts with the members of the Institute, with the purpose of familiarizing the candidate with the charism of the order and with the obligations of the novitiate. This contact will be carried out by one or several priests, as designated by the Provincial Superior, who must know the candidate, his vocation and his suitability, in order to present him to the novitiate.

237 The duration of the postulancy is not fixed but depends on the candidate’s preparation, his level of Christian and human maturity, his basic general culture, his emotional balance, and his capacity to live in community, etc.,282 because “most of the difficulties found nowadays in the formation of novices come from the fact that they don’t have the minimum necessary maturity when admitted to the novitiate.”283 So that “nobody will be admitted without adequate preparation,”284 this period is required. Postulancy will not last more than two years.

Article 3: Novitiate

238 Life in the Institute begins in the novitiate. The novitiate lasts for one year. “The novitiate, through which life in an institute is begun, is arranged so that the novices better understand their divine vocation, and indeed one which is proper to the institute; so that they experience the Institute’s way of life, and form their mind and heart in its spirit; and so that their intention and suitability are tested.”285

239 The candidate’s Provincial Superior admits him into the novitiate, wherein the novices286 must duly prepare themselves to make their profession according to the demands of religious life. The Institute scrutinizes the candidate to receive him into its bosom.

1st one who has not yet completed the seventeenth year of age;

2nd a spouse, while the marriage is still valid;

3rd one who is currently bound by a sacred bond to an institute of consecrated life, or is incorporated into a society of apostolic life;

4th one who enters the Institute through force, fear or deceit, or whom the superior accepts under the same influences;

5th one who has concealed his incorporation in an institute of consecrated life or society of apostolic life.

2. The admission of clerics or others who had been admitted to another institute of consecrated life, to a society of apostolic life, or to a seminary, also requires the testimony of the local Ordinary, the major superior of the Institute or society, or the rector of the seminary, according to necessity.

3. The superiors can seek other information, even without informing the candidate, as they deem necessary.

3. The Provincial Superior may permit a group of novices to reside in another specified house of the Institute for a certain period of time.

243 1. In order to be valid, the novitiate must consist of twelve months spent in the novitiate community.

2. To complete the formation of the novices, we establish one or more periods of apostolic activity, to be performed outside the novitiate community.

3. A novitiate is invalidated by a continuous or interrupted absence from the novitiate house for more than three months. Any absence of more than fifteen days must be made up.

4. With the permission of the Provincial, first profession may be done in advance, though not by more than fifteen days.

244 “A novice may freely leave the institute. The competent authority of the institute may also dismiss a novice,”287 without prejudice to what is said in can. 653 § 2.

245 Spiritual formation must prevail in the novitiate, as must intellectual formation for the novices, such that they may pursue further studies. However, pastoral experiences, especially missionary ones, can also be carried out according to the charism proper to the Institute.

246 The novices are under the care of a Master named by the Superior General with the deliberative vote of the Council. Another priest can be added as Vice-Master according to necessity.288

247 The governance of the novices is reserved solely for the Master of Novices, under the authority of the Provincial Superior.

248 Dialogue with the Master of Novices: Dialogue with the Superior is a privileged time during the formation period. It benefits the novice as well as the temporally professed members. It favors the good of the community. In this trust-filled dialogue, the religious informs his superior about all the activities he is carrying out. If he wishes, he may reveal the state of his conscience as well. It is advisable to dialogue twice a month during the novitiate. (This practice is also advisable once a month after profession until perpetual profession, and frequently thereafter.)

249 The Master of Novices must encourage the novices to live human and Christian virtues, and bring them along a path of greater perfection through prayer and self-denial; he must instruct them in the contemplation of the mystery of salvation and in the reading and meditation of Sacred Scriptures. He must prepare them for the celebration of God’s worship in the Sacred Liturgy, form them to live a consecrated life to God and to all men in Christ through the evangelical counsels, and instruct them in the character, spirit, purpose, discipline, history, and life of the Institute; he will strive to infuse in them love for the Church and her holy shepherds.289

250 After an assessment period, the novices will receive the religious habit.
