Article 5: Religious Seminary a. Seminary for Religious Who Are Candidates to the Priesthood

258 The Institute of the Incarnate Word is a clerical institute, wherein the majority of the members are priests. Upon finishing the novitiate, a new period of priestly formation begins, executed according to Canon Law for the formation of clerics and according to the documents of the Holy See, and always in accordance with the spirituality and mission of the Institute, so as to accomplish an authentic overall formation: human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral.

259 According to our own charism, we strive to orient all our studies toward the evangelization of the culture, for which we will spare no efforts or means. We are not content with a merely superficial knowledge of philosophy and theology that is incapable of understanding the modern exercise of atheism in all its depth, and is thus incapable of providing a remedy for it.

b. Seminary of the Coadjutor Brothers

260 The Institute will also have religious called “coadjutor brothers.” They will dedicate themselves to serving the houses and to giving spiritual services that do not require the sacramental grace of Holy Orders.

261 These brothers should complete formation in the seminary, where they will take some courses in philosophy and theology, “attending to the needs of the Church and the circumstances of men and the times, according to the end and the character of the Institute.”292 The coadjutor brothers will continue their formation, under the direct authority of the local superior, until their perpetual profession in the houses to which they are assigned. Their ongoing formation must be monitored.

Article 6: Ongoing Formation

262 Religious life is a process of continual conversion that does not end with the years of formation, but must be maintained and must grow every day.293 Regarding our pastoral work, this formation is an act of true and proper justice for God’s people, who always demand the most appropriate answer from us.294

263 Ongoing formation, not limited by the age or circumstances of the member, possesses four dimensions: human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral.

264 We believe that permanent and ongoing formation is fundamental. To accomplish this, in addition to ordinary measures such as conferences, retreats, courses, exams, etc., extraordinary measures should be taken whenever possible, for example: the 30day spiritual exercises every ten years, pilgrimages to the Holy Land and to great shrines of Christianity, etc.

265 In order to undertake this ongoing formation, we desire that all the members of our Institute take ecclesiastical or civil courses after the Seminary, according to their capacities and talents. These will be taken preferably in the pontifical universities of Rome or in those institutions recognized by the Holy See, so as to receive the qualifying degree of licentiate and doctorate.295 We already have a priestly community in Rome where two years are normally spent for this purpose.296 The formation in Rome implies the attainment of a Roman spirit, which entails a “crown of virtues: universal openness, fidelity to the Magisterium, a missionary spirit, endurance, and magnanimity.”297 Being in Rome is a “situation that permits [one] to live the supernatural reality of communion with the Church of Rome and with the Bishop of Rome. In the ecclesiastical experience [one] enters into the field of a new reality: [one] experiences the communion with all who are in communion with the Church of Rome.”298 Therefore, the opportunity to study in the Eternal City has a two-fold advantage: “It means having the advantage of living in a community either of priests or seminarians, and having access to the scholarship available in or through the Roman universities. It means being witnesses, day after day, to the living tradition of the faith as it is proclaimed in the See of Peter.”299

266 Therefore, the Church of Rome is the best place for this formation: “There is no other place with such an opportunity to form suitable priests as there is in the center of Christianity, next to the tombs of the two great Apostles, under the paternal solicitude of the Supreme Pontiff, who by his function as Vicar of Christ, is the common Father of all people and guardian and interpreter of the Catholic faith.”300

Roman-ness is “understood as the special spirit of communion with the Successor of Peter, visible Head of the Church of Christ, by means of unity of faith, and charity.”301

These studies can also be undertaken in any scholastically prominent civil university according to the judgment of the Superior General and his Council.

267 Every superior should use any means necessary for all members of the community to obtain this ongoing formation: conferences, retreats, courses, exams, etc. We must spend our whole life searching for the full truth: “If truth is not longed for with all the strengths of one’s soul, it cannot be found in any way.”302

Article 7: Those Responsible for the Formation

268 We will take special care preparing and choosing those priests in charge of the formation of seminarians, as the future of the Institute depends on it. This is what we mean by “to form a school”: that those priests in charge of the formation of our future priests must be able to transmit the heritage of our Institute, as opposed to forming a “solitary” priest, that is, one who would not contribute to the continuation of our work. In the work of evangelizing the culture, the efforts of one individual or one generation are not sufficient; rather, a great evangelical movement is necessary, one that will forever deepen and extend itself in this task. This is the work of those responsible for formation. Therefore, those in charge of formation must be formed themselves as men of suitable discernment who are rich in spirit.

269 Besides sufficient knowledge of Catholic doctrine regarding faith and morals, the task of forming others demands certain conditions. These conditions are: human intuition and warmth, familiarity with God and prayer, wisdom, love for liturgy, necessary cultural competence, availability, and willingness to dedicate personal care to each of the seminarians individually, and not merely to the group. To accomplish this, one must have interior serenity, availability, patience, understanding, and true affection toward those who have been commended to him.303

Article 8: Re-admission

270 Anyone who may have legitimately left the Institute upon completing the novitiate, or even after profession, may be re-admitted by the Superior General with the consent of his Council, with no obligation to repeat the novitiate. The Superior General will determine the appropriate testing prior to temporary profession, as well as the duration of the vows prior to perpetual profession.304

PART 8 GOVERNMENT OF THE INSTITUTE

Introduction: The Religious Family of the Incarnate Word

271 The Institute of the Incarnate Word recognizes the primary and supreme authority of the Supreme Pontiff, and professes not only obedience to him, but also fidelity, filial submission, adherence, and disposition for the service of the universal Church.

272 Ever docile to the will of God, superiors will regard the exercise of their authority as true service to the Church and will always remember that the primary obligation of the superior is to command well.

Article 1: Female Branch: The Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará

273 Both “the Institute of the Incarnate Word” and its female branch, “the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará” form the “Religious Family of the Incarnate Word.” Both Institutes are indissolubly united. Their union is spiritual, though legally independent. Their spiritual union is given essentially through possessing the same founder and twin Constitutions, by the Spiritual Father (elected by the women religious), and by the help of other priests of the Institute of the Incarnate Word (spiritual advisers, community advisers, spiritual directors, confessors, professors, etc.) who are appointed for these tasks by the competent authority.

Article 2: Contemplative Branch

274 The male contemplative branch is also part of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. It is comprised of those houses where the religious dedicate themselves to the contemplative life in conformity with the provisions of proper law.

275 Every monastery should have a superior designated by the Superior General with the consent of his council.

276 The monasteries are houses of the Institute belonging to the province in whose territory they are located.

Article 3: Third Order

277 The Institute of the Incarnate Word also has a Third Order. Third Order “members live in the world but share in the spirit of … [the] institute, under… [its] overall direction…”305

278 The Third Order is structured on three levels, according to the degree of commitment which the members freely choose:

- First Degree: Lay associates who aspire to evangelical perfection according to the spirit of the Institute by participating in its mission,306 obligating themselves freely through private vows or some other sacred bond. - Second Degree: Lay associations of the faithful: groups or movements, each with its own structure, that want to participate in the spirit and purpose of the Institute.

- Third Degree: All faithful lay people related in different ways to the Institute, who want to share in its spirit: friends, acquaintances, benefactors, family members, etc.

279 The Third Order is united to and dependent upon our Religious Family in both aspects, in groups and individually.

280 The Superior General, with the deliberative vote of his Council, chooses the Major Adviser, the liaison between the Institute and the Third Order. Each Provincial Superior, in conjunction with the Provincial Superior of the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará, is the liaison in his province, and gives spiritual assistance to the tertiaries, according to the three levels of the Third Order.

Article 4: Central Coordinating Board

281 The Superior General of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, or his delegate, will preside over the Central Coordinating Board, made up of: the Superior Generals of both Institutes; the superiors of each Institute, Movement, and Association of the Third Order. This board will coordinate the different apostolates, the foundations, the promotion of the spirit of the Institutes, etc. It will not possess any competence in the government of any branch.

CHAPTER 1 DIVISION OF THE INSTITUTE

282 The houses of the Institute will be grouped into provinces, vice-provinces, and delegations that can be established by the General Chapter and the Superior General together with his Council “ad referendum” of the General Chapter.

283 When a homogeneous group of houses does not meet the minimum conditions to constitute a province, then a viceprovince or a delegation can be established, according to the degree of development it may have reached. The vice-provinces and the delegations will be governed by a superior who possesses the necessary faculties and who is appointed by the Superior General with the consent of his Council.

CHAPTER 2 GENERAL CHAPTERS

284 The supreme governing body of the Institute of the Incarnate Word is the General Chapter, which shall be convoked according to the time and form established below.

Article 1: Convocation of the Chapters

285 General Chapters can be either ordinary or extraordinary.

The General Chapter is convoked ordinarily every six years in order to elect the Superior General and to deal with all matters established in canon 631 § 1, and other matters that may be necessary. Likewise, it is convoked extraordinarily to hold a new election on account of the death, resignation, or removal307 of the Superior General.

Pending due consent of his Council, the Superior General may convoke an Extraordinary Chapter to address grave matters of the utmost importance to the Institute.

286 The General Chapter will be convoked and presided over by the Superior General or his substitute. Also attending, with voice and deliberative vote, will be the following:

1) By reason of office:

- The former Superior Generals of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. - The General Councilors. - The Provincial Superiors and others who are their equals - The Rectors of the Major Seminaries. - The Rectors of duly established Clerical Colleges.

2) Delegates by Election:

- Priests under perpetual vows from each province and viceprovince, in proportion to the number of members of each jurisdiction, elected by an absolute majority of the perpetually professed members. The numerical proportion must be established in a pre-Chapter regulation.

- Two superiors of monasteries – for every six monasteries – elected as the Directory of Contemplative Life dictates.

With regard to the capacity and conditions of the voters and the votes, we will take into account what is established in Canon Law.308

287 The number of Delegates by Election of the General Chapter must be higher than that of the Participants by Reason of their Office.

Article 2: Celebration of the Chapter

288 The President of the Chapter is the Superior General of the Institute or one who takes his place.

289 The Chapter Fathers will secretly vote for a Chapter Secretary, two auxiliaries and two auditors.

290 A profession of faith according to can. 833 will be made at the opening of the General Chapter. The General Secretary will then immediately record in the minutes the names of those in attendance. In the same way, he will record the name of the person elected Chapter Secretary, auxiliaries, and auditors. He will also record the agenda of the day.

291 At a suitable time, the Chapter will proceed to elect the Superior General by a vote that is free, secret, certain, and absolute, and by a two-thirds majority vote of the Chapter Fathers present. After two inefficient audits wherein the two-thirds majority has not been reached, there will be a third vote between the two candidates who obtained the highest number of votes; or, if there are more than two, the election will be held between the two longest professed; or, if they are equal in length of period of profession, the election will be between the two oldest. After the third audit, if a tie persists, the longest professed will be elected, and if they are equal in this amount of time, the older will be elected.309 The Superior-elect will be notified immediately. From that moment, the Superior-elect will have a period of eight working days to accept or reject the position, and if he accepts, to name the Vicar General, the General Secretary, and the Treasurer. Those designated by the Superior General will likewise have an equal length of time to accept or reject the appointment.

292 After electing the Superior General, the Chapter will proceed to elect, by absolute majority, two members who will be part of the General Council, and then to elect the first, second, and third substitute Councilors, also by absolute majority. In the event that the Superior General’s nominations include any members already elected by the Chapter to be Councilors or Substitutes, the nominations by the Superior General will take priority, and he himself will fill the missing positions. The members of the General Council, elected by the Chapter, will remain in their functions for the same period of time as the Superior General, and both the Superior General and council members can be re-elected.310

293 Once the elections have been verified, the Chapter will hold the necessary sessions in which the new Superior General will be informed of the state of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. The other religious in attendance can make observations about things that they think are worthy of consideration for the well-being of the provinces and houses of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

294 The main matters that will be addressed within the General Chapter are:

1) The defense of the patrimony of the Institute of the Incarnate Word; making adjustments and implementing renewal according to it, electing the Superior General, and promulgating the rules that bind for all Institute members.311

2) The amendment of a given point of the Constitutions, by a two-thirds consent of the General Chapter members, which then must be approved by the competent ecclesiastic authority.312

3) The revision and modification of the general Directories,313 Regulations, and other rules.

4) The division of the Institute as a whole into provinces, viceprovinces, and delegations,314 and the cessation of the same.315

5) Definition of the way in which the evangelical counsels will be observed.316

6) The handling of any other major topics, requests, and suggestions that may be freely contributed.317

CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General

295 The Institute is permanently governed by a Superior General assisted by his Council of five Councilors. Of the six members of the General Government, the Superior General and at least two Councilors will be elected by the Chapter. The Vicar General, the General Secretary, and the General Treasurer are named by the Superior General.

296 The Superior General holds the highest rank in the Institute and exercises the functions of primary authority. He attends to the care and government of the Institute of the Incarnate Word and of all its members according to the present Constitutions and Canon Law.

The Superior General’s jurisdiction of authority is over the entire Institute of the Incarnate Word and over each of its members, both in the apostolic and contemplative houses.

To be elected and to perform this office, he must possess ability, discretion, prudence, maturity, and the other virtues required for the sound performance of his duty.

To be elected, the Superior General must be a priest with at least fifteen years of perpetual profession318 in the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

He is elected for a period of six years and can be reelected.

297 - The voters must be careful not to elect anyone who has desired or sought the office of Superior General. The same applies for choosing the other superiors.

298 - The Superior General must avoid preferential treatment of members of the Institute. He must have the same attitude toward everyone, and avoid showing partiality. Preference of persons is a sin that opposes distributive justice – the principle of giving positions, offices, and responsibilities for the common good in proportion to the dignity or ability of each person. In justice, the person who is most suitable for each assignment must be chosen for the common good. Therefore, the person’s qualifications regarding his suitability must be considered. When we fail to do so, we commit the vice of partiality of persons. The person chosen in such a case is appointed because of who he is, and not because of his abilities; he therefore prevents the one who, in justice, should fill that office from doing so. This kind of injustice is expressly prohibited in Sacred Scripture.319 The Superior should be a father in the image of the Heavenly Father, Who shows no partiality (Acts 10:34).

299 - The Superior General is expected to be faithful to the Constitutions. He should not grant himself the authority to exempt anyone from honoring them even for minor reasons.

300 - He is never to reprimand in anger. He is to be gentle with all and strict with himself. He is never to speak in praise of himself except with the hope of bringing about some good, and even then only with humility and acknowledgment of God’s gifts.

301 - All functions and obligations flowing from his office as Superior General must be performed with a spirit of exceptional service. His authority is for service and his service is authoritative. He is to govern as one who serves, because he is obligated by reason of his office to serve by leading: Let the greatest among you be as the youngest, and the leader as the servant (Lk 22:26).

302 Faculties and duties of the Superior General are:

1st To govern the members as sons of God. The Superior General is to extend to them the same paternal charity that God has for them. He is also to have that fraternal charity desired by God in loving the other superiors and members. God also desires that they too love each other with the same fraternal charity.

2nd To respect each human person because of his dignity as a person, and even more so because of the added dignity flowing from baptism and consecration. Moreover, he is to respect them because of the combination of inborn and acquired abilities which make up the uniqueness of each member.

3rd To promote voluntary obedience, to foster willingness in obedience and submissive freedom. Whoever has freely professed obedience must voluntarily practice the specific acts of that counsel. The perfect attainment of this ideal will be the supernatural and human sign of the proper exercise of authority.

4th To listen willingly. To listen is neither to assent, nor to hear with deaf ears; neither is it the attention of a disciple, nor the instruction of a teacher. Listening does not require giving an answer, for indeed, an answer may not exist. Nor may it be prudent or obligatory to give any answer. Nor is it his duty to reach an agreement on what he and any member may have been talking about, as this agreement is often non-existent or impossible to attain. Nor is it his duty to make a decision that accommodates the desires of a member.

5th To foster his initiatives for the good of the Institute and the Church, because he is obligated to do so by his office, he must energetically resist any passivity, as if merely waiting for others to suggest initiatives.

6th To decide and to order what should be done, taking into account the executive power given by Canon law.320

303 The specific and proper functions of the Superior General, besides the ones already established by can. 619 of CIC, are the following:

1st To work for the preservation and growth of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

2nd To promote members’ knowledge and observance of the Holy See’s decrees relating to religious.

3rd To oversee observance of the Constitutions and fidelity to the spirit of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

4th To promote as much as possible the spiritual and temporal good of all the members of the Institute, and to ensure that everyone fulfills his respective duties and obligations.

5th To preside over the sessions of the General Council and present therein all the matters to be addressed. The Superior General can seek advice from the Council any time he deems it necessary.

6th To notify the Provincial Superiors, and when he deems it appropriate, to directly notify the Local Superiors, of the Council’s resolutions that they should be aware of.

7th To visit all of the Provinces and houses of the Institute for inspection and general direction.

8th To oversee all aspects of the spiritual and intellectual formation of religious.

9th To convoke ordinary and extraordinary General Chapters, according to these Constitutions.

10th To grant the license to publish writings related to religious or moral matters.321

11th Within the limits of his proper competence, the Superior General can grant dispensations, that is, relaxations of merely ecclesiastical laws in a particular case,322 in every place, with respect to the members, and with respect to himself,323 according to the conditions demanded by Canon law.324

304 The Superior General also possesses other duties which he must execute together with his Council as determined in Chapter 4 (The Office of the General Chapter).

305 The Superior General can be removed from his office for the reasons stated in the Code of Canon law.325

Article 2: Members of the General Council a. Vicar General

306 He is the second in authority in the Institute, whom all religious are obliged to obey after the Superior General. He will exercise his authority according to these Constitutions only when he replaces the Superior General or carries out the functions delegated by him.

307 The appointments that are under the competence of the Superior General cannot be made by the Vicar General.

308 In the case of vacancy or absence, the Vicar General can be replaced by whomever the Superior General designates.

309 The priest who performs this office should have the necessary abilities and must be perpetually professed at least 10 years in the Institute.

310 The Vicar General can be removed from his office for the same reasons as the Superior General. The same applies for all other superiors.326

311 In addition to his obligations as Vicar General, he, as first General Councilor, will substitute for the Superior General in his absence, illness, or other impediments. Likewise, in case of death, resignation, or removal of the Superior General, the Vicar will temporarily undertake the governance of the Institute. However, the Vicar General may neither proceed to a new election, nor transfer, nor appoint any Provincial or Local Superior except in the case of necessity, for four months from the date of vacancy. After those four months, the Vicar General cannot defer the convocation for the election of the Superior General for longer than three more months.

b. Secretary General

312 This office will be performed by a priest with at least 10 years of perpetual profession in the Institute. He must also possess the qualities required by this office.

313 It is incumbent on the Secretary General:

- To record the minutes of Council sessions and those of the General Chapters.

- To send out all communications of the Superior General re-garding matters of the Superior General’s office.

- To take care of and update all of the Institute’s records concerning persons, houses, provinces, dealings with civil and religious organizations, contracts, statistics, etc.

c. Treasurer General

314 The priest to whom the office of Treasurer General is given must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute and be qualified for this job.

315 The Treasurer General is responsible for the administration of the Institute under the authority of the Superior General and the supervision of his Council. He will take particular care of all documentation concerning goods and their custody.

316 The Treasurer General will register all income and expenses of funds and valuables. He will inform the Council regarding the state of the above-mentioned matters every three months and whenever the Council requires.327

d. Other General Councilors

317 In addition to the priests already mentioned, two more priests will form part of the General Council. They will be given the name of General Councilors.

318 These priests must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute and have the prudence and all the other virtues necessary for the exercise of their office together with the other members of the Council.

319 To replace the General Councilors appointed by the Superior General, the Superior General himself will make the new appointments. The same applies to the replacement of those provincial or local councilors appointed by the provincial or local superior, respectively.

320 Whenever any Councilor from those elected by the General Chapter ceases to belong to the General Council because of resignation, removal, transfer, or any other cause, he will be re-placed by the first substitute, and successively thereafter.

CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties

321 The General Council acting as a college. The Superior General is first among his equals with the same right to vote. The decision must be made as a college,328 and therefore its execution is binding for the members of the General Council. The college will be convoked according to can. 166 and requires a quorum of four. It is responsible for:

- approval of the Directories of the Institute, ad referendum of the General Chapter; modification of those Directories already approved, as needed, and also ad referendum of the General Chapter, to adapt them to the Church Magisterium’s new documents. Modification of the Directories is necessary to update them according to the new documents of the Magisterium of the Church. Any modification to the Directory of Monasteries will require two-thirds consent of the perpetually-professed members of the Contemplative Branch.

- Decree of dismissal by absolute majority of the present members.329

322 The General Council acting with deliberative vote. The Council acts according to can. 127, § 1 from the CIC, not as a college, but rather as a group of persons from whom consent is required. Decisions will be made by an absolute majority of those present. The final action will be the result of the personal choice and authority of the Superior, who may act according to the mentioned decision, or abstain from acting. The Council will be convoked as established in can. 166 of CIC, and will decide on:

- The establishment of provinces, vice-provinces and delegations ad referendum of the next General Chapter.

- The appointment of Provincial Superiors, vice-provincials, and delegates. The appointment should be preceded by appropriate consultation.330 Individuals must be notified of the offices for which they have been appointed; they may accept or refuse their respective offices within a period of eight working days.

- The appointment of superiors of houses of formation, namely, both major and minor seminaries, masters of novices, rectors of universities, and superiors of monasteries, after having consulted the Provincial Superior.

- The agreement upon and the appointment of the priest elected by the female branch to be its spiritual father.

- The appointment of the major adviser of the Third Order.

- Admission to the diaconate and priesthood.

- The establishment of houses.331

- The establishment or cessation of novitiates,332 major seminaries, minor seminaries, and other houses of formation.

- The cessation of houses.333

- The approval of study plans for the houses of formation. - Material transactions.334

- The exception of making the novitiate in a different house.335

- Change of institute.336

- The exclaustration of perpetually professed priests.337

- The indult of departure to temporarily professed religious.338

- The re-admission of ex-members.339

323 The General Council acting with consultative vote. The Council acts as a group; everyone’s advice or opinion is necessary for an act to be valid. The final action will be the result of the personal choice and authority of the Superior, who can act even against what is unanimously advised if he has sufficient reason for doing so. The Council will be convoked according to Canon law340 to deal with the following matters:

- Approval of local regulations for the houses of formation and monasteries.

- Approval of other general regulations.

Article 2: Meetings of the General Council

324 There will be two kinds of general council meetings: ordinary and extraordinary, both of which will be presided over by the Superior General, and in his absence, by the Vicar General or whoever takes his place.

325 Ordinary meetings will be held each month, and the extraordinary meetings will be held when needed. Matters concerning the Institute will be dealt with and resolved in both types of meetings. Such matters will be presented by whoever presides. For meetings to be valid, a quorum of three is needed, except for what is established in paragraph 321 of these Constitutions.

326 Council members have the right to present proposals concerning the following topics: formation, apostolate, discipline, spiritual life, and other proposals, all of which should be recorded in the minutes.

327 Council members should present their opinions with fidelity and sincerity, and give their consent in matters of great importance.

328 Except for cases in which the Council acts collegially, the Superior is outside and above his Council, which means that he is not to vote when consultation or consent are required as a group of persons,341 or as individual persons.342

329 During the first three months of the year and in an ordinary meeting, the income and expense accounts of the Institute’s general administration will be submitted for examination and approval.

330 Within the first three months of the year, the Institute’s Provinces and Houses are to prepare and submit the annual income and expense accounts of the previous year to the General Council; this does not prevent the Superior General or the Provincial Superior from examining the accounts of the provincial or local administrations on the occasion of the ordinary or extraordinary canonical visit.

331 The Councilors are rigorously warned to keep all matters addressed during meetings confidential. Only the Superior General can communicate decisions with due discretion when appropriate.

CHAPTER 5 THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Provinces

332 To make governance of the Institute easier and more effective, territorial divisions called provinces are permanently established, according to the various conditions of people, places and time.

333 The General Chapter, and the Superior General ad referendum of the General Chapter, are responsible for the establishment or modification of province and vice-province boundaries, in accordance with established norms. The following norms must be considered:

a) In order for a territory or a group of houses to constitute a province, at least three canonically established houses of the Institute of the Incarnate Word are required.

b) As far as possible, homogeneity of the territory and its socio-cultural features will be taken into account, as will access to communications and administrative conveniences.

334 Under the direction of the Superior General and his Council, each province is governed by a Provincial Superior, assisted by four provincial Councilors.

Article 2: Provincial Superior

335 The priest appointed Provincial Superior must have the necessary physical and moral aptitude to execute the demands of this office, and must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute. The General Superior, with the consent of his Council, can dispense with this condition.

336 The Provincial Superior is appointed for three years, and may be reappointed for another three years in the same province, but ordinarily his appointment will not exceed this amount of time.

337 The Provincial Superior will exercise his authority over each and every house in the province under his jurisdiction, and also over the monasteries of contemplative life established in the same territory.

338 The faculties and obligations of the Provincial Superior are:

1st To exercise authority in the province, under the authority of the Superior General whose directives he will faithfully execute and whom he will appropriately inform regarding the life of the province.

2nd To appoint the first two members of the Provincial Council, that is, the vicar and the secretary.

3rd To appoint the local superiors with the consent of his Council.

4th To preside over the sessions of the provincial council and to propose the matters to be addressed therein. He can consult his council whenever he deems it necessary.

5th To communicate to the local superiors the resolutions and decrees that he receives from the general and provincial councils.

6th To resolve matters proposed by the house superiors or by religious, and also, according to the importance of these matters, to forward any appropriate issues to the Superior General and his Council.

7th To transmit to the Superior General all news and reports which will help him in appointing members for the positions that are under his competence.

8th To visit the houses of his province once a year and as many times as necessary.

9th To admit candidates to the novitiate and to temporary profession, after having consulted his Council. Similarly, to extend the period of temporal profession, with the consent of his Council.343

10th To admit candidates to perpetual profession with the consent of the provincial council.

11th To exclude members from subsequent profession, after consulting his Council.344

12th To grant permission for a prolonged absence from the community.345

13th To grant permission in particular cases regarding the individual goods of those who are professing according to what is established in n. 70 of these Constitutions.346

339 For the Superior General to be well-informed on the life and progress of the Institute, at the end of each year the Provincial Superiors will send an exact and detailed account on the financial and disciplinary state of the province and its government (in addition to the ordinary reports), together with the annual personal letter.

340 The Superior General, with the deliberative vote of his Council, will be able to grant the Provincial Superiors wider faculties within the norms of Canon law, principally to those located further away. However, those faculties granted to Provincial Superiors, ordinary as well as extraordinary, can in no way limit the authority and rights that belong to the Superior General and his Council according to the Constitutions.

Article 3: Members of the Provincial Council a. Provincial Vicar

341 The Provincial Vicar is appointed directly by the Provincial Superior. He shall exercise his authority over all members of the province when he substitutes for the Provincial Superior. He can also act with the functions delegated by the Provincial Superior.

342 In addition to possessing the aptitude required of his office, the Provincial Vicar must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute. After consulting his Council, the General Superior can dispense with this condition.

b. Provincial Secretary

343 The provincial secretary is directly appointed by the Provincial Superior. He will perform the functions of secretary and provincial filing clerk, and the preservation of provincial documents as well as those of the provincial government archive will be entrusted to his care. For appointment to this office, the priest must have made perpetual vows.

c. Other Provincial Councilors

344 The other provincial councilors, apart from the required aptitude for the office, must be religious with perpetual vows. They will be elected by the religious with perpetual vows who belong to the province (they will also elect three substitute councilors). When the majority of those who have been convoked are present, members who have the absolute majority of votes will be elected. After two inefficient audits, there will be another vote between the two candidates who obtained the highest number of votes; if there are more than two candidates, the election will be between the two longest professed. If they share the same amount of time professed, the election will be between the two oldest; after the third audit, if a tie persists, the longest professed will be elected, and if the candidates are equal in this, the older will be elected.

345 The provincial councilors will remain in their office for three years. Upon completion of their term, they can be reelected, but not normally for a third three-year term.

d. Provincial Treasurer

346 The Provincial Superior will choose the provincial treasurer from the two councilors. The priest so-appointed must possess the necessary ability to faithfully execute his office.

347 The administration and custody of the province’s goods belong to the provincial treasurer under the authority of his superiors. He will ensure the accuracy of all documents and ledgers of income and expenses. He will present his reports to the Provincial Superior and his council for their knowledge, revision, and approval every three months, and whenever required by competent authority.

Article 4: Provincial Councils

348 The faculties and obligations of the provincial council are:

a) To handle cases within their competence, by means of consultative or deliberative vote, according to the rules of Canon law and the Institute’s proper law.

b) To examine and approve the accounts of the province.

c) To give the consultative vote for the admission of candidates to the Novitiate and temporary profession, and to give its consent for the admission of candidates to perpetual profession, by absolute majority of the quorum.

349 The provincial council must be convoked once a month and can convene for extraordinary sessions whenever the Provincial Superior, or his substitute, deems it appropriate. For validity, a session requires a quorum of two members in addition to the Provincial Superior. What is established in n. 328 applies to the Provincial Superior.

CHAPTER 6 CANONICAL VISITS

350 The Superior General must make an official visit to every province and house of the Institute at least once during his mandate, and whenever necessity demands it; unofficially, he must do so when he deems it appropriate.

351 In the event that he cannot perform this grave duty, he himself will appoint a religious as visitor.

352 By reason of his office, the Provincial Superior will visit each house of his province on three different occasions during his term of office, and as many times as special circumstances require.

CHAPTER 7 THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT

353 Each house must have a sufficient number of religious to ensure community life and the practice of the evangelical counsels.347 That is why at least three religious must be assigned, except in special cases.

354 In every local community of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, there must be a priest who carries out the office of the local superior, assisted by a council with four members (except where this is not possible because of the number of priests), the first two of whom shall be directly elected by the local superior and who shall carry out the office of local vicar and secretary, re-spectively. The rest of the members shall be elected by simple majority of the priests who belong to the same community. One of them shall be elected by the local superior for the office of local treasurer.

Article 1: Local Superior

355 The superior is the head of the family in each house; all the religious in that community must obey his orders with docility, exactness, and religious submission.

356 Naming a local superior must be preceded by appropriate consultation.348 To be appointed local superior, the religious must be a priest with perpetual vows, and must possess the ability to govern, a spirit of religiosity, a spirit of observance, and other re-quirements for the office.349

357 His term of office will be three years, and ordinarily he will not be reappointed for a third consecutive term in the same house.

358 The local superior has the following duties and tasks:

1) To govern the community, keeping in mind the purpose of religious life and the particular goals of the Institute.

2) To oversee the observance of the Constitutions; to see to it that the spirit of the Institute of the Incarnate Word is maintained; and to dispense with some point of discipline in particular cases for a reasonable cause and in accordance with the norms established by the major superiors of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

3) To promote the knowledge and observance of decrees of the Holy See related to religious, or those of interest among the community’s religious.

4) To name the second councilor, when possible, and to consult his immediate major superior, and those responsible for the various offices. Those who have been named will be notified, and they will have eight working days to accept or decline the office.

5) To regulate what he deems conducive to the order and service of the household, and whatever leads to the greater good of the family entrusted to his care and concern.

6) To preside over all activities of the house.

7) To resolve grave and urgent cases when it is impossible to appeal to the general or Provincial Superior, and to give an account of his resolution afterward to the competent major superior, indicating the motives for the resolution in question.

8) To meet with his councilors once a month and whenever necessary for their input, so that he may resolve what he deems more appropriate in the Lord. To be valid, the meeting must be attended by at least two members of the local council.

9) To write the local regulations with his council that will be submitted for approval of the Provincial Superior, except when the regulation must be approved by the Superior General according to proper law.

359 In cases requiring consultation and whenever else he deems it appropriate, he will contact the Provincial Superior. He will also submit to him an accurate report of the state of the house and its members at least every three months. He will also write to the Superior General at least once a year and as many times as he deems it necessary.

Article 2: Local Councilors

360 The first local councilor is also the vicar and substitutes for the superior during his absence, illness, or other impediment, outside of which he does not have any authority except for what the superior delegates to him. In the vicar’s absence, the councilor who is next in line will substitute for the local superior, according to the established order.

361 The second councilor, directly appointed by the local superior, will be the filing clerk responsible for handling and maintaining the house files.

362 A priest will hold the office of local treasurer in each house of the Institute; he will administer the goods of the house under the direction of the local superior. In fulfilling his duties he will oversee the funds and valuables that belong to the community. The local treasurer administers the goods of the community and is responsible for making ordinary purchases, according to the norms established by the local superior; he will carefully do the bookkeeping, and will give a report to the council of the house every month, every three months to the Provincial Superior, and as requested.

363 Besides possessing the necessary aptitude, those priests appointed for the local council350 must have taken perpetual vows. They remain in office for a renewable three-year term.

364 Local councilors are obligated to maintain complete confidentiality regarding the matters about which they are consulted. However, they must honestly inform the general or Provincial Superior if required to do so.

PART 9 ADMINISTRATION OF GOODS

365 The goods of the Institute are the goods of the Church. Therefore, their administration must be according to Canon Law, these norms, and the Institute’s proper law. The Institute, as a juridical person,351 has the right to purchase, possess, administer, and sell temporal goods, according to Church Canon law.352

366 Ultimately, the Superior General is responsible for all of the Congregation’s goods.

367 The Treasurer General, acting under the authority of the Superior General, administers all the goods of the Institute.

368 The respective treasurers administer the goods of the Institute, provinces, and houses under the authority of their immediate superiors, who will be informed of all matters concerning these goods.353

369 The treasurers are to provide a regular account from their administration to their corresponding superior.

370 When acquiring assets, any resources consistent with the life of the Institute should be implemented, according to what is determined by the administration’s regulations.

371 The Superior General’s written consent will be re-quired to validate any act of disposing of or administering goods that has grave significance to the Institute.

372 “Any appearance of luxury, immoderate profit and accumulation of goods is to be avoided.”354

373 Something will be set aside, as means allow, for the needs of the Church and sustenance of the poor.355

PART 10 SEPARATION FROM THE INSTITUTE

374 The norms of Canon law will be followed in the case of separation from the Institute:

375 Transfer to another Institute: CIC, cc 684-685.

376 Departure from the Institute: CIC, cc 686-693.

377 Dismissal of members: CIC, cc 694-704.

PART 11 OBLIGATION TO OBSERVE THE CONSTITUTIONS

378 All members of the Institute must observe the evangelical counsels with the greatest possible perfection. They must also surrender to Jesus through Mary, and “direct their lives according to the Institute’s own law and so strive for the perfection of their state.”356

379 The Institute’s proper law is formed by: the Constitutions handed down by the founder; the Directories containing subsidiary and practical norms, which serve to apply the Constitutions; the Rules and Chapter norms and documents; the executive decisions of the superiors; traditions, good customs, and proper documents.

380 May the Blessed Virgin Mary help us all to reach the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

“God alone.”357
